q: בן 78, אושפז לברור עקב קושי בבליעת מוצקים וירידה במשקל. הועלה חשד לקרצינומה של הוושט. מהם גורמי הסיכון לאדנוקרצינומה של הוושט בגיל המבוגר?
o: טיפול ממושך ב- PPI's
שתיית אלכוהול
רקע של Barrett esophagus
אכלזיה
explanation:
Distinguish **esophageal adenocarcinoma from squamous cell carcinoma**: their risk factors differ. Barrett esophagus is associated with adenocarcinoma, whereas the established alcohol association is mainly with squamous cell carcinoma; risk factors should not be transferred between histologies (Hazzard 8e, p. 1449; Freedman et al., Abstract, Background and aims and Conclusions).
"In contrast to ESCC, higher alcohol consumption was not associated with increased risk of either EA or EGJA." (Freedman et al., Abstract, Conclusions)

**A. Long-term PPI treatment.** Wrong, Hazzard does not support increased malignant transformation risk in Barrett esophagus from long-term PPIs; it describes an observational association with lower risk. PPIs treat reflux, so distinguish treatment from the disease for which it is prescribed (p. 1322, Figure 85-9 and histologic-changes discussion).
**B. Alcohol consumption.** Wrong, the BEACON analysis found no increased adenocarcinoma risk with higher alcohol consumption, unlike the established association with squamous cell carcinoma. It is therefore not the matching histology-specific risk factor (Freedman et al., Abstract, Background and aims and Conclusions).
**C. A history of Barrett esophagus.** Correct, Hazzard describes Barrett-associated adenocarcinoma, which is the association tested by the officially selected option (p. 1449).
**D. Achalasia.** Wrong, not accepted by the official key, but the source distinction matters: achalasia is associated mainly with squamous cell carcinoma, and the source also describes a smaller increase in adenocarcinoma risk. Achalasia therefore does not exclude adenocarcinoma; Barrett esophagus is the direct association officially selected (Vaezi et al., Endoscopic Surveillance for Cancer, journal p. 1407).

The official key and bank select a history of Barrett esophagus: Barrett esophagus is associated with esophageal adenocarcinoma (Hazzard 8e, p. 1449).
Note: The general risk-factor wording does not distinguish Barrett's direct association from the increase also described with achalasia. This explanation preserves official scoring and explicitly states the overlap (Vaezi et al., Endoscopic Surveillance for Cancer, journal p. 1407).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1322, 1449; Freedman et al. Alcohol intake and risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma: a pooled analysis from the BEACON Consortium. Gut. 2011;60:1029–1037, Abstract, Background and aims and Conclusions, doi:10.1136/gut.2010.233866; Vaezi et al. ACG Clinical Guidelines: Diagnosis and Management of Achalasia. Am J Gastroenterol. 2020;115:1393–1411, Endoscopic Surveillance for Cancer, journal p. 1407, doi:10.14309/ajg.0000000000000731. Articles checked in full-text HTML; no PDF-page locator asserted.

q: A comprehensive geriatric assessment team has implemented a care plan and is following the patient. Progress toward the agreed goals is inadequate. Which response is part of the CGA process described in Hazzard?
o: Maintain the plan and judge success by the number of documented problems
Complete follow-up and judge success by the number of recommendations delivered
Reassess the plan with the patient and monitor the effects of revisions
Expand the plan and judge success by the number of specialist referrals
explanation:
**Monitoring in CGA** assesses progress toward the agreed goals. When progress is inadequate, the team reevaluates the patient, revisits recommendations and implementation, involves the patient, and monitors changes (p. 130).
"Treatment recommendations and implementation plans may need to be revised." (p. 130).

**A. Maintain the plan and judge success by the number of documented problems.** Wrong, detecting problems has not consistently improved outcomes; inadequate progress calls for reassessment (p. 130).
**B. Complete follow-up and judge success by the number of recommendations delivered.** Wrong, delivering recommendations does not establish progress toward goals, and revisions require further monitoring (p. 130).
**C. Reassess the plan with the patient and monitor the effects of revisions.** Correct, this follows the sequence of reevaluation, patient engagement, revision, and further monitoring (p. 130).
**D. Expand the plan and judge success by the number of specialist referrals.** Wrong, more referrals do not establish progress; recommendations should be prioritized for the desired outcomes (p. 130).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 130.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p.130

q: A 76-year-old woman with dementia, diabetes, and hypertension undergoes comprehensive geriatric assessment. Her adult son is her principal caregiver. Which approach best incorporates patient-centered care into the treatment plan?
o: Use motivational interviewing to secure agreement with goals already chosen by the team
Use motivational interviewing to identify her priorities and willingness to make changes
Use the diagnosis list to set disease-based goals before discussing the plan with her son
Use her son's preferences to set goals and judge success by adherence to instructions
explanation:
**Patient participation** helps the team align the plan with the person's priorities. Hazzard states: "Through techniques such as motivational interviewing, patients can be asked to identify their priorities and willingness to make changes" (p. 130). The patient and appropriate family members should be included in developing the plan whenever possible (p. 130).

**A. Use motivational interviewing to secure agreement with goals already chosen by the team.** Wrong, this uses the interview to secure agreement rather than elicit the patient's priorities as the source describes (p. 130).
**B. Use motivational interviewing to identify her priorities and willingness to make changes.** Correct, this elicits the priorities and readiness that the source uses to make patients active partners in care planning (p. 130).
**C. Use the diagnosis list to set disease-based goals before discussing the plan with her son.** Wrong, a plan fixed from diagnoses before discussion omits the patient's role in establishing priorities (p. 130).
**D. Use her son's preferences to set goals and judge success by adherence to instructions.** Wrong, the source includes appropriate family members alongside the patient; substituting the son's goals omits her participation (p. 130).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 130.
ref: Hazzard Ch 8 — PRINCIPLES OF GERIATRIC ASSESSMENT

q: A 76-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is undergoing a trial without catheter. He has difficulty voiding and a postvoid residual of 650 mL. Glucose and oxygen saturation are normal, and he is stable. Which action addresses this residual according to the bladder-retraining protocol in Hazzard?
o: Reinsert a Foley catheter and plan another voiding trial
Lengthen the intervals between voids and monitor a bladder diary
Start a bladder relaxant and monitor urinary symptoms
Reduce daily fluid intake and remeasure the residual later
explanation:
**A large postvoid residual** during a voiding trial calls for drainage in the source protocol. Bladder relaxants are considered for frequency or urgency when residuals are low, not for this degree of retention (p. 711). "If the postvoid residual is > 300–400 mL, then catheterize with a Foley catheter and plan another voiding trial in a few days." (p. 711).

**A. Reinsert a Foley catheter and plan another voiding trial.** Correct, the measured residual exceeds the protocol range prompting Foley catheterization and a later trial of voiding (p. 711).
**B. Lengthen the intervals between voids and monitor a bladder diary.** Wrong, delaying voiding is described for frequent voiding after checking for adequate emptying; this patient has a large residual requiring drainage (p. 711).
**C. Start a bladder relaxant and monitor urinary symptoms.** Wrong, a trial of a bladder relaxant is described when residuals are low, which is not the finding here (p. 711).
**D. Reduce daily fluid intake and remeasure the residual later.** Wrong, reducing intake does not perform the drainage called for by the high-residual branch of the protocol (p. 711; application to this case).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 711.

q: An 81-year-old woman has lost about 8 lb and feels fatigued over recent months. She lives with her daughter, who works full time, and spends most days alone watching television and eating microwave meals. BMI is 19.5 and albumin 3.1 g/dL; PHQ-2 is negative, and the Berkman-Syme social network index indicates marked isolation. Which plan directly addresses mealtime isolation as part of nutritional care?
o: Provide oral nutritional supplements to consume alone at home.
Arrange delivered meals to consume alone at home.
Provide an appetite stimulant while maintaining solitary meals.
Arrange shared lunches through a senior-center meal program.
explanation:
**Mealtime companionship** is relevant to nutritional care: the source associates eating alone with lower energy intake and social company with greater nutrient intake. Applying that principle, shared meals address the isolation described without claiming they are proven to be the most effective intervention for this patient (p. 410). "Eating alone may be associated with a lower energy intake, and the presence of family and close friends leads to greater nutrient intake." (p. 410).

**A. Provide oral nutritional supplements to consume alone at home.** Wrong, supplementation may address intake, but consuming it alone leaves the identified mealtime isolation unchanged (p. 410; inference).
**B. Arrange delivered meals to consume alone at home.** Wrong, delivery may provide food, but the stated solitary setting does not address mealtime companionship (p. 410; inference).
**C. Provide an appetite stimulant while maintaining solitary meals.** Wrong, maintaining solitary meals leaves the social issue unchanged; Hazzard also notes that appetite stimulants such as cyproheptadine have not shown effectiveness in older adults (pp. 410, 428).
**D. Arrange shared lunches through a senior-center meal program.** Correct, shared lunches provide company at meals, directly applying the source's social-nutrition principle to the identified isolation (p. 410; inference).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 410, 428.
ref: Hazzard Ch 30 — NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION
chapterTitle: NUTRITION DISORDERS, OBESITY , AND ENTERAL/PARENTERAL ALIMENTATION

q: An 88-year-old woman with advanced COPD is seen in palliative care. She uses continuous oxygen and a wheelchair and needs assistance with all activities of daily living. Because of treatment burden, she asks to stop her medications, including prednisone taken daily for two years. What approach applies if chronic prednisone is discontinued?
o: Stop prednisone and monitor for recurrent respiratory symptoms
Stop prednisone and restart it if fatigue develops
Taper prednisone gradually to allow adrenal-axis recovery
Stop prednisone and reserve replacement for a future illness
explanation:
**Chronic corticosteroid withdrawal** requires a taper because the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis needs time to recover. The source states that tapering is necessary "in order to allow the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis to recover and to avoid adrenal crisis." (p. 1532).

**A. Stop prednisone and monitor for recurrent respiratory symptoms.** Wrong, waiting for respiratory symptoms after abrupt withdrawal does not implement the taper required to permit adrenal-axis recovery (p. 1532).
**B. Stop prednisone and restart it if fatigue develops.** Wrong, waiting for fatigue after abrupt withdrawal does not prevent the adrenal-crisis risk for which a taper is recommended (p. 1532).
**C. Taper prednisone gradually to allow adrenal-axis recovery.** Correct, this follows the stated reason for tapering chronic corticosteroids rather than abruptly withdrawing them (p. 1532).
**D. Stop prednisone and reserve replacement for a future illness.** Wrong, a plan for future illness does not replace the taper needed during current discontinuation of chronic corticosteroid therapy (p. 1532).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1532.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: חולה הנוטה למות שהיא בעלת כשרות מסרבת להארכת חייה, ומוצע לה טיפול שגרתי בזיהום נלווה. מהי הגישה לפי סעיף 15 לחוק?
o: להסיק שסירוב להארכת חיים מחייב מניעת כל טיפול
לכבד רצון ולעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנע לקבל טיפול
להתחיל טיפול בזיהום בהתעלם מהסירוב שהביעה
להעביר לבני המשפחה את ההחלטה במקום החולה
explanation:
החוק מבחין בין **כיבוד רצון החולה** לבין החובה לעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנע לקבל טיפולים נלווים ומקלים. אין לתרגם הגבלת טיפול להארכת חיים למניעה גורפת של טיפול, וגם אין בכך היתר להתעלם מסירוב של חולה בעלת כשרות (עמ׳ 10, סעיף 15).
"חולה הנוטה למות שהוא בעל כשרות, אשר אינו רוצה שחייו יוארכו, יש לכבד את רצונו ולהימנע מטיפול רפואי בו." (עמ׳ 10).
"על המטפלים בחולה הנוטה למות כאמור בסעיף קטן (א) לעשות מאמץ סביר כדי לשכנעו לקבל חמצן," (עמ׳ 10).

**א. להסיק שסירוב להארכת חיים מחייב מניעת כל טיפול.** שגויה, הסעיף מחייב מאמץ לשכנע לקבל טיפול נלווה ומקל, ולכן אינו מורה על מניעה גורפת (עמ׳ 10).
**ב. לכבד רצון ולעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנע לקבל טיפול.** נכונה, שני חלקי התשובה משקפים את החובות המשלימות בסעיף (עמ׳ 10).
**ג. להתחיל טיפול בזיהום בהתעלם מהסירוב שהביעה.** שגויה, הוראת השכנוע אינה מבטלת את החובה לכבד את רצונה (עמ׳ 10).
**ד. להעביר לבני המשפחה את ההחלטה במקום החולה.** שגויה, במקרה של חולה בעלת כשרות ההוראה היא לכבד את רצון החולה עצמה (עמ׳ 10).

מקור: חוק החולה הנוטה למות, תשס_ו-2005.pdf, עמ׳ 10.
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: An 83-year-old woman with COPD experiences dyspnea during rehabilitation. Which breathing modification is described in Hazzard as a way to reduce the sensation of breathlessness?
o: Pursed-lip breathing with a shortened exhalation phase
Pursed-lip breathing with a prolonged exhalation phase
Open-mouth breathing with a shortened exhalation phase
Faster-rate breathing with a shortened exhalation phase
explanation:
**Breathing techniques** are among the nonpharmacologic approaches to dyspnea. Hazzard lists “pursed lip breathing, prolonged exhalation, and posture modification” among techniques that can reduce the sensation of dyspnea (p. 1074). These measures can be considered alongside pharmacologic treatment as first-line approaches (p. 1074).

**A. Pursed-lip breathing with a shortened exhalation phase.** Wrong, pursed lips match one listed technique, but shortening exhalation conflicts with the prolonged exhalation specified by the source (p. 1074).
**B. Pursed-lip breathing with a prolonged exhalation phase.** Correct, both pursed lips and prolonged exhalation are source-described techniques for reducing breathlessness (p. 1074).
**C. Open-mouth breathing with a shortened exhalation phase.** Wrong, shortened exhalation does not implement the prolonged-exhalation technique asked for (p. 1074).
**D. Faster-rate breathing with a shortened exhalation phase.** Wrong, increasing the rate with shortened exhalation does not implement the source’s prolonged-exhalation approach (p. 1074).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1074.
ref: Hazzard Ch 69 — MANAGEMENT OF COMMON NONPAIN SYMPTOMS

q: Tramadol is being considered for an older patient who takes an antidepressant and has renal failure. Which pair of considerations matches Hazzard's medication table?
o: Reduced serotonergic risk and adjustment of the dose for renal failure
Reduced serotonergic risk and continuation of the usual renal dose
Serotonin syndrome risk and adjustment of the dose for renal failure
Serotonin syndrome risk and continuation of the usual renal dose
explanation:
**Tramadol requires attention to drug interactions and renal dosing**. The table flags serotonin syndrome with SSRIs or other antidepressants and separately calls for dose adjustment in renal failure (p. 1653). "May cause serotonin syndrome in combination with SSRIs or other antidepressants" and "Dose adjustment for renal failure" (p. 1653).

**A. Reduced serotonergic risk and adjustment of the dose for renal failure.** Wrong, renal adjustment is appropriate, but the combination raises concern for serotonin syndrome rather than reduced serotonergic risk (p. 1653).
**B. Reduced serotonergic risk and continuation of the usual renal dose.** Wrong, this misses both the interaction warning and renal adjustment specified in the table (p. 1653).
**C. Serotonin syndrome risk and adjustment of the dose for renal failure.** Correct, both components correspond to the antidepressant exposure and renal failure in the stem (p. 1653).
**D. Serotonin syndrome risk and continuation of the usual renal dose.** Wrong, recognizing the interaction does not remove the separate need for renal dose adjustment (p. 1653).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1653.
ref: Hazzard Ch 103 — FIBROMYALGIA AND MYOFASCIAL PAIN SYNDROMES

q: בת 75, ברקע. דמנציה, דיכאון, סוכרת, יתר לחץ דם ואוסטאוארטריטיס. התקבלה למחלקה לרפואה דחופה. עקב החמרה בתפקודי כליה בבדיקות המעבדה נמצאה אי ספיקה כלייתית עם קריאטינין 2.3 ו- BUN - 70. בבדיקה לפני חצי שנה- קריאטינין 1.2 ו- BUN תקין. מתוך כל התרופות שלקחה בביתה – כולן יכולות לגרום לאי ספיקה כלייתית חדה פרט ל-
o: Etoricoxib ( ארקוקסיה)
Empagliflozin ( ג'רדיינס)
Candesartan ( אטקנד)
Ecitralopam ( ציפרלקס)
explanation:
**Drug-associated kidney injury** may result from impaired renal perfusion or volume depletion. The source describes relevant mechanisms for NSAIDs, renin-angiotensin system blockers, and SGLT2 inhibitors in appropriate settings; this does not establish which drug caused this patient's deterioration without further evaluation (Hazzard 8e, pp. 1280, 1288, 1580).
"These agents increase urine volume and sodium excretion" (SGLT2 inhibitors, p. 1580).

**A. Etoricoxib (Arcoxia).** Wrong, for official scoring. The inherited explanation applies the NSAID mechanism of reduced glomerular perfusion and filtration, especially with renin-angiotensin system blockade. The checked passage supports that class mechanism but does not identify etoricoxib by name (p. 1280).
**B. Empagliflozin (Jardiance).** Wrong, it increases urine and sodium excretion and may cause volume depletion. This is a possible mechanism for deterioration in a vulnerable setting, not a claim that every treated patient develops kidney injury (p. 1580).
**C. Candesartan (Atacand).** Wrong, blocking angiotensin-dependent autoregulation can reduce filtration, for example with hypoperfusion or renovascular disease (p. 1288).
**D. Escitalopram (Cipralex).** Correct, according to the official key. Mechanistic comparison (inference): its described serotonin-reuptake mechanism differs from the renal mechanisms used for the other choices; the label requires no dose adjustment in mild or moderate renal impairment. This is not a guarantee that it can never be associated with a renal event (escitalopram prescribing information, sections 6.2, 8.7, 12.1).

**Official answer: ד** — Escitalopram (Cipralex), inherited answer declaration.

Note: Acute renal failure appears among postmarketing reports in the label, which cautions that such reports cannot always establish frequency or causality. The question's exception must therefore not be interpreted as an absolute absence of risk (escitalopram prescribing information, sections 6.2, 8.7, 12.1).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1280, 1288, 1580; DailyMed, escitalopram prescribing information, 2026, sections 6.2, 8.7, 12.1, https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=f2b3b385-658d-5918-e053-2a95a90afcba.

o: התעוררות מהירה לאחר האירוע
כאבי שרירים
טשטוש ראיה לפני האירוע
פעילות מוטורית של פחות מ- 10 שניות
explanation:
**Post-event myalgia** favors seizure in the article's comparison, but is not diagnostic by itself. The prodrome, movement pattern and recovery must be considered together because syncope can also include involuntary movements (Lee, 2019, Differential Diagnosis and Table 3).
“Brief myoclonic jerks or tonic posturing is common in cases of syncope.” (Lee, Differential Diagnosis).

**A. Rapid awakening after the event.** Wrong, appropriate behavior and orientation usually return rapidly after syncope, whereas prolonged confusion favors seizure (Hazzard 8e, p. 670; Lee, Table 3).
**B. Muscle pain.** Correct, the table describes myalgia as common with seizure and rare with syncope, making it the best-fitting finding among these options without implying absolute specificity (Lee, Table 3).
**C. Blurred vision before the event.** Wrong, visual disturbances may occur in the prodrome of syncope and therefore do not preferentially identify seizure here (Hazzard, pp. 669–670).
**D. Motor activity lasting less than 10 seconds.** Wrong, brief movements can also occur in syncope. Short duration alone is not evidence of seizure, and the number in the option should not be turned into an absolute diagnostic threshold (Hazzard, p. 669; Lee, Differential Diagnosis and Table 3).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 669–670; Lee SK. Epilepsy in the Elderly: Treatment and Consideration of Comorbid Diseases. J Epilepsy Res. 2019;9:27–35. doi:10.14581/jer.19003, Differential Diagnosis and Table 3.

q: בן 80, נמצא במעקב מרפאת אי-ספיקת לב. ידוע על מחלת לב אסכמית. עבר אירוע לב לפני כ- 4 שנים, באקו לב תפקוד לב ירוד עם מקטע פליטה של 35%. בבדיקתו: ללא בצקת פריפרית, ללא סימני גודש ריאתי. אשפוז אחרון בעקבות החמרה באי-ספיקת לב לפני מספר חודשים. המטופל מתעניין לגבי פעילות גופנית. מה ההמלצה במצבו?
o: פעילות גופנית יכולה להחמיר תפקוד חדר שמאל ולכן לא מומלצת
פעילות גופנית יכולה לשפר תפקוד ותחושת well being אבל לא משפרת קוצר נשימה
פעילות גופנית יכולה לשפר איכות חיים ולהוריד תמותה
פעילות גופנית מומלצת במצבו היא חיזוק שרירים בלבד ולא פעילות אירובית
explanation:
Official answer: ג

In **stable heart failure with reduced ejection fraction**, supervised exercise improves quality of life, physical function, aerobic capacity and symptoms. The cited source also reports lower mortality and readmission with supervised aerobic exercise. Absence of congestion in this case supports suitability for cardiac rehabilitation (pp. 808, 830; application to the case).

**A. Exercise may worsen left ventricular function and is therefore not recommended.** Wrong, historically activity was restricted for this concern, but excessive restriction causes deconditioning. Controlled rehabilitation trials improved exercise tolerance, quality of life and symptoms without adverse effects on left ventricular function (pp. 1177, 830).
**B. Exercise improves function and well-being but not dyspnea.** Wrong, training adaptations reduce exercise intolerance from fatigue and dyspnea; rehabilitation improved shortness of breath, activities of daily living and general well-being (p. 830).
**C. Exercise can improve quality of life and reduce mortality.** Correct, this is the official answer, supported by the described quality-of-life benefit and the association of supervised aerobic training with reduced mortality and readmission in chronic heart failure (pp. 808, 830).
**D. Strength training only, without aerobic activity.** Wrong, the source supports regular aerobic and/or strengthening exercise. Supervised aerobic training is associated with reductions in mortality of 35% and hospital readmission of 28% in chronic heart failure (pp. 808, 830).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 808, 830, 1177.

q: מה נכון בנוגע לטיפול בתרופות אדג'ובנטיות לטיפול בכאב כרוני בזקנים?
o: תרופות ממשפחת ה- Tricyclics מהוות קו ראשון לטיפול בכאב נוירופתי
ל- Venlafaxine יתרון בטיחותי במניעת נפילות ושברים
לטיפול ב- Carbamazepine סיכון להיפונתרמיה
טיפול ב- Gabapentin מחייב מעקב הדוק אחר רמות תרופה בדם
explanation:
Official answer: ג

**Carbamazepine can cause hyponatremia**, requiring sodium monitoring as well as serum drug levels. When selecting adjuvant analgesics for older adults, anticholinergic burden and fall risk also matter (pp. 1063–1065).

**A. Tricyclics are first-line treatment for neuropathic pain.** Wrong, they can be effective, but strong anticholinergic activity and risks of confusion and falls do not support presenting them as a blanket first-line choice in older adults (pp. 1063–1064).
**B. Venlafaxine has a safety advantage in preventing falls and fractures.** Wrong, venlafaxine is an SNRI; the source cautions against this class in people with prior falls or fractures, so it does not establish the proposed protective advantage (pp. 1063–1064).
**C. Carbamazepine carries a risk of hyponatremia.** Correct, the table explicitly identifies this risk, and the text requires sodium monitoring when treatment is initiated (pp. 1063, 1065).
**D. Gabapentin requires close monitoring of blood drug levels.** Wrong, the source describes low-dose initiation, titration and adverse-effect monitoring for gabapentin. Its explicit serum-level requirement concerns carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, not gabapentin (pp. 1063–1065).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1063, 1064, 1065.

q: An older inpatient develops delirium after several psychoactive medications are added. Which interpretation best explains why these drugs need review?
o: Medication effects and interactions represent a potentially remediable precipitant of delirium.
Medication effects and interactions usually leave a persistent, nonremediable cause of delirium.
Increasing the number of prescribed drugs tends to reduce delirium through offsetting effects.
Drug interactions explain delirium better because the drugs themselves lack direct effects.
explanation:
**Medication burden** contributes to delirium through direct effects and drug–drug and drug–disease interactions (p. 882). Medication review addresses a potentially reversible precipitant: “medications often incite delirium, they are also the most common remediable cause of delirium.” (p. 882).

**A. Medication effects and interactions represent a potentially remediable precipitant of delirium.** Correct, review targets both direct effects and interactions as potentially reversible contributors (p. 882).
**B. Medication effects and interactions usually leave a persistent, nonremediable cause of delirium.** Wrong, the source specifically describes medication exposure as the most common remediable cause (p. 882).
**C. Increasing the number of prescribed drugs tends to reduce delirium through offsetting effects.** Wrong, delirium incidence increases with the number of prescribed drugs; extra agents do not provide the proposed protection (p. 882).
**D. Drug interactions explain delirium better because the drugs themselves lack direct effects.** Wrong, excluding direct effects misses one of the mechanisms explicitly identified by the source (p. 882).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 882.

q: An older community-dwelling person reports a stair fall during the past year and performs poorly on a balance test. Which next step follows the chapter’s approach?
o: Use the initial screening score to select the intervention before assessing contributing deficits.
Assess contributing deficits further to develop an individualized fall prevention care plan.
Schedule reassessment after a second fall to establish the need for a prevention care plan.
Use a predictive TUG cutoff to select the intervention after documenting the fall history.
explanation:
**Fall history and impaired balance or gait** identify people who need further assessment (p. 637). They “should be assessed further to develop an individualized fall prevention care plan.” (p. 637); identifying underlying deficits guides interventions.

**A. Use the initial screening score to select the intervention before assessing contributing deficits.** Wrong, screening identifies people who need comprehensive assessment; interventions should be guided by underlying deficits that this sequence has not yet evaluated (p. 637).
**B. Assess contributing deficits further to develop an individualized fall prevention care plan.** Correct, a fall history and impaired balance meet the indication for further assessment and an individualized plan (p. 637).
**C. Schedule reassessment after a second fall to establish the need for a prevention care plan.** Wrong, the indication includes one or more falls with poor balance or gait. Waiting for another fall delays assessment already indicated here (p. 637).
**D. Use a predictive TUG cutoff to select the intervention after documenting the fall history.** Wrong, the cited review could not recommend a TUG cut-point for predicting falls; that unsupported boundary cannot replace evaluation of contributing deficits (p. 637).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 637.

q: בת 72, פליטה מאוקראינה, ללא היסטוריה רפואית ידועה, לדבריה בריאה בדרך כלל, לא שותה הרבה אלכוהול, וללא טיפול תרופתי קבוע. הופנתה בשל הרגשה כללית רעה מזה 2-3 ימים. בבדיקות הדם הפרעה משולבת באנזימי כבד. אילו מהממצאים הבאים מכוונים לכך שמדובר בהפרעה ממושכת, ולא אקוטית?
o: רמת ALT גבוהה יותר מאשר AST.
הפרעה בתפקודי קרישה
רמה תקינה של אמוניה
רמת אלבומין מתחת ל 3 gr/dL
chapterTitle: Harrison 22e ch. 348 – Evaluation of Liver Function
keySource: IMA 2024-Sep Basic official answer key after appeals, Q124
explanation:
**Official answer:** D (IMA 2024-Sep Basic official answer key after appeals, Q124).

**Official source:** Harrison · ch. 337 · p. 2555.

Albumin below 3 g/dL raises concern for chronic liver disease. Its 18-20-day half-life makes a substantial reduction less consistent with an isolated two-day hepatic illness, although hypoalbuminemia has other causes (p. 2635).

**A. ALT higher than AST.** Wrong, this enzyme relationship can occur in acute hepatocellular injury and does not establish chronicity (p. 2637).
**B. Coagulation abnormality.** Wrong, clotting factors turn over rapidly, so prolonged PT can reflect acute severe synthetic failure as well as chronic disease (pp. 2636-2637).
**C. Normal ammonia.** Wrong, ammonia correlates poorly with liver function and encephalopathy and is not a reliable duration marker (p. 2636).
**D. Albumin below 3 g/dL.** Correct, slow albumin turnover makes this a clue to a pre-existing process; the chapter explicitly recommends considering chronic disease at this level (p. 2635).

Source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition, chapter(s) 348, pp. 2635-2637.
